# Numerical Methods for Physicists

A course on how a physicist solves problems that have no analytic solution. One lecture is one physical problem: the pendulum and chaos, a chain of oscillators, electrostatics, heat conduction, waves, quantum mechanics, cosmology, hydrodynamics, radiative transfer. The methods needed (eigenproblems, sparse systems, the FFT, spherical harmonics, the SVD) are introduced when a problem cannot be solved without them. The language is Python with Numba.

## Course lectures

::: {.lecture-accordion}

<p class="course-kicker">Preparation</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">01</span><span>Python, NumPy and Numba</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The random walk ($\langle x^2\rangle=N$) and $\pi$ by Monte Carlo: why numerical methods are needed, what numerical error and convergence are, how to trade accuracy against time.

**Tools:** Jupyter, NumPy arrays, slicing and broadcasting, data types and precision, a seeded random number generator, Matplotlib, timing, Numba; Python versus Mathematica.

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<p class="course-kicker">Part I. Equations, matrices, motion</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">02</span><span>Roots and quadratures</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The period of a pendulum at large amplitude (an elliptic integral) and the energy levels of a finite well (a transcendental equation): the exact answer is known, and one sees how numerical methods converge to it.

**Tools:** bisection, Newton's method, secants; rectangles, trapezoids, Simpson, Gaussian quadrature; order of convergence, singular integrands.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">03</span><span>Ordinary differential equations: the pendulum</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The pendulum beyond small oscillations; the reference is the energy and the period from lecture 2. First the method works, then one sees where and why it fails.

**Tools:** Euler, Runge–Kutta and Verlet schemes, order of accuracy and convergence test, adaptive step, events (impact, dry friction), stiffness and implicit Euler.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">04</span><span>Eigenvalue problems: normal modes</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

A chain of $N$ masses and phonons; random masses lead to localization. The limit $N\to\infty$ gives the wave equation.

**Tools:** `eigh`, spectral decomposition, matrix functions (the evolution operator), tridiagonal matrices, the condition number.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">05</span><span>Chaos and synchronization</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The double pendulum, the restricted three-body problem, Kuramoto oscillators. Why an «exact» solution of a chaotic system is impossible and what counts as a result then.

**Tools:** adaptive Runge–Kutta methods (`solve_ivp`), the Lyapunov exponent, Poincaré sections, the order parameter, trajectory ensembles with Numba.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<p class="course-kicker">Part II. Fields, diffusion and waves</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">06</span><span>Electrostatics: the Poisson equation and multipoles</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The potential of conductors in a box (the reference is a capacitor and a Fourier series); a non-conducting sphere with charge density $\sigma(\theta,\varphi)$: the field inside and outside, exact via spherical harmonics.

**Tools:** sparse matrices, LU and Cholesky, Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and conjugate gradient iterations, the multipole expansion, $Y_{\ell m}$, Gauss–Legendre quadrature.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">07</span><span>Diffusion and random forces</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Cooling of a rod (the reference is the Green function), nonlinear and inhomogeneous media; a Brownian particle under a random force, continuing the random walk of lecture 1.

**Tools:** explicit and implicit schemes, von Neumann stability, the tridiagonal (Thomas) algorithm, Crank–Nicolson, the method of lines, the Langevin equation (Euler–Maruyama scheme).

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">08</span><span>Waves and the telegraph equation</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

A string (the reference is d'Alembert's solution) and a lossy transmission line (Heaviside's signal): the third type of equation after Poisson and heat conduction.

**Tools:** characteristics, the Courant condition, numerical dispersion, absorbing boundaries.

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">09</span><span>Fourier analysis and the FFT</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Frequencies in a noisy signal; solving the diffusion and wave equations in Fourier space; the momentum representation in quantum mechanics.

**Tools:** the FFT, aliasing, windows, convolution, spectral derivatives.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<p class="course-kicker">Part III. Quantum mechanics</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">10</span><span>Stationary quantum mechanics</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The oscillator (reference), the anharmonic oscillator, the double well, the hydrogen atom; scattering on a barrier.

**Tools:** the Hamiltonian as a matrix, shooting, Numerov, the variational method, the transmission coefficient, convergence of levels.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">11</span><span>Quantum evolution and neutrino oscillations</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Wave packets and tunnelling; $2\nu$ oscillations (exact) and $3\nu$ oscillations in matter of varying density.

**Tools:** Crank–Nicolson and unitarity, split-step with the FFT, the matrix exponential (`expm`).

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<p class="course-kicker">Part IV. Data and statistical physics</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">12</span><span>Interpolation and approximation</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

Reconstruct a function from points when the function itself is known (the reference), and see why more nodes are not always better.

**Tools:** the Lagrange polynomial, the Runge phenomenon, Chebyshev nodes, splines, least squares, the danger of extrapolation.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">13</span><span>Monte Carlo in statistical physics: the Ising model</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The two-dimensional Ising model: the phase transition, the critical temperature and thermodynamic quantities; the reference is Onsager's exact solution.

**Tools:** the Metropolis algorithm, autocorrelation and errors, finite-size effects, heat capacity and susceptibility, Numba acceleration.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">14</span><span>Inverse problems: the reactor antineutrino spectrum and the SVD</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The positron spectrum is measured, the antineutrino spectrum is needed: a response matrix with detector resolution and its inversion.

**Tools:** the singular value decomposition, the condition number, the pseudo-inverse, truncated SVD and Tikhonov regularization, deconvolution.

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<p class="course-kicker">Part V. Flows, transport and machine learning</p>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">15</span><span>Hydrodynamics: shock waves and vortices</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The Burgers equation (the reference is the Hopf–Cole solution), the Sod shock tube (a Riemann problem); briefly, Taylor–Green vortices.

**Tools:** conservative schemes, finite volumes, the Godunov scheme, limiters, the pseudo-spectral method.

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">16</span><span>The transport equation: from Boltzmann to light in water</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

A photon in a turbid medium: ballistics, diffusion (lecture 7), finite speed (lecture 8). The example is light in Lake Baikal and a neutrino telescope.

**Tools:** Monte Carlo for transport, the diffusion approximation, expansion in angular moments ($P_N$).

**Lead author:** Dmitry V. Naumov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
<details class="lecture-row">
<summary><span class="lecture-index">17</span><span>Machine learning for differential equations</span></summary>

<div class="lecture-row-body">

The oscillator and the heat equation with known solutions: what a neural network gives and what it costs compared with classical methods.

**Tools:** a neural network as an approximator, physics-informed networks (PINN), comparison with classical methods in accuracy and cost.

**Lead author:** Kirill Bazarov.

<div class="lecture-links">
<span class="lecture-link-pending">in preparation</span>
</div>

</div>
</details>
